## Names and EIDs:

-   Amanda Lee, awl646

# Introduction:

This analysis will look at water quality data from the City of Austin's Open Data Portal. It is collected to assess water quality conditions in the natural creeks, aquifers, and lakes in Austin and surrounding areas. Citizens have a right to know more about their water quality. Especially given that we, as students, use the same water everyday. Therefore, learning more about the water quality could give actionable insights into how to make better water decisions.

![A picture of Barton Springs, one of Austin's significant groundwater aquifers. Taken from <https://www.austintexas.org/listings/barton-springs-pool/4687/>.](https://assets.simpleviewinc.com/simpleview/image/upload/c_limit,q_75,w_1200/v1/crm/austin/011-421ace03bc29117_421acf68-dde1-a643-f8d4f8148337c3cd.jpg)

In an article from Inside Climate News, author Martha Pskowski writes that "there are 224 public water supply wells that are considered contaminated", according to the Texas Groundwater Protection Committee's annual report. For a growing state with less and less surface water sources, this issue is one that cannot be ignored if Texas hopes to continue to attract new residents. Water quality testing extends to agriculture as well. As the "largest consumer of groundwater statewide", the agricultural sector's handling of water quality impacts the diet of every Texan.

The data set to be analyzed can be found here: <https://data.austintexas.gov/Environment/Water-Quality-Sampling-Data/5tye-7ray/about_data>.

Each row is a water quality sample by parameter, date, and location in Austin, TX. We are primarily interested in variables watershed, site_type, and result to understand the distribution of water quality across Austin. The following research questions are investigated in this report:

-   **How do bacteria/pathogen concentrations vary by time of day and type of water source? (Nabil)**

-   **How do bacteria/pathogen concentrations vary by site type in terms of safeness? (Amanda)**

# Method

```{r global_options, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE,  
                      warning = TRUE, message = FALSE, 
                      fig.align = "center",
                      R.options = list(max.print=100))

library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
# Importing 2024 Austin water quality sampling data set 
water <- read.csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Amandawlee/sds322_project/refs/heads/main/Water_Quality_Sampling_Data.csv')

# Data tidying/wrangling
water_tidy <- water |>
  # Rename columns to lowercase
  rename_all(~ str_to_lower(.)) |>
  # Select all relevant columns
  select(data_ref_no, watershed, site_type, site_name, sample_date, lat_dd_wgs84, lon_dd_wgs84, param_type, parameter, result, method, medium, unit) |>
  # Remove any missing NA values with selected columns
  na.omit() |>
  #Filter out since only contained in one observation
  filter(parameter != 'HETEROTROPHIC PLATE COUNT') |>
  # Filter out coordinates that are not in Austin
  filter(lon_dd_wgs84 != 0 | lat_dd_wgs84 != 0) |>
  mutate(date = mdy_hms(sample_date), year = year(date))

head(water_tidy)
```

There are 1,475,965 rows and 24 columns in the original data set. Much of this data is unconcerned with dangerous chemicals or pathogens and thus we have limited the data set to bacteria/pathogen samples through the City of Austin open data portal since this has one of the most hazardous effects on health. The data set 'water' contains 34,893 rows and 24 columns.

Additionally, the data was tidied/wrangled with the following changes or omissions. The resulting data set 'water_tidy' contains 32,758 rows and 15 columns.

1.  All column names were converted to lowercase.

2.  Only 15 relevant columns out of 24 were selected for analysis (data_ref_no, watershed, site_type, site_name, sample_date, lat_dd_wgs84, lon_dd_wgs84, param_type, parameter, result, method, medium, unit).

3.  Any missing NA values within the selected columns were removed.

4.  The parameter 'HETEROTROPHIC PLATE COUNT' was filtered out since there was only one observation.

5.  Any observations with a latitude or longitude coordinate of 0° will be excluded, as these coordinates do not fall within the Austin area.

# Results

## Bacteria/Pathogen Concentration Changes Over Time Per Source

To begin to see the variations in bacteria/pathogen concentrations between ground and surface water concentrations, we must first investigate the distributions of each variable involved. We'll first look at the counts of the types of water sources.

```{r}
water_tidy |>
  ggplot() + #Make bar plot of water sources w/o legend
  geom_bar(aes(y = medium, fill = medium), show.legend = F) +
  labs(
    x = 'Number of Sources',
    y = 'Type of Source',
    title = 'Distribution of Water Sources',
    caption = 'Figure 1: Distribution of water sources in Austin, TX'
  ) + 
  theme_bw()

water_tidy |> #Calculate summary statistics (counts) for water sources
  group_by(medium) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```

From Figure 1 and the summary statistics, the three largest sources are 1704 storm water sources, 9161 ground water sources, and 22531 surface water sources. Moving forward, storm water sources will not be included for analysis since they have wildly different bacteria concentrations and cannot be controlled by community intervention. Next, we'll look at the distribution of bacteria concentration across all sources. This will include the following bacteria: total coliform bacteria, fecal streptococci, fecal coliform bacteria, E coli bacteria, and enterococcus. Total coliform bacteria is filtered out since it only accounts for a single row and happened only one time. The EPA recommends that for a domestic water supply that is to be treated, concentrations for the previously mentioned bacteria should be less than 2000 colonies per 100 milliliters. Therefore, the visualization only looks at bacteria concentrations in excess of 2000 colonies/100 mL.

```{r}
water_tidy |>
  filter(result >= 2000 & result < 10000) |> #Only look at concentrations above 2000 colonies/100 mL and less than 10000 to see general trend
  ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = result, fill = parameter), show.legend = F, binwidth = 1000, center = 500) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter) +
  labs(
    x = 'Concentration of Bacteria (Colonies/100 mL)',
    y = 'Frequency',
    title = 'Distribution of the Relative Concentrations of Bacteria',
    caption = 'Figure 2: Distribution of the relative concentrations of bacteria in Austin, TX'
  ) + 
  theme_bw()

  

water_tidy |> #All units are colonies/100 mL
  group_by(parameter) |>
  summarize(mean_concentration = mean(result),
            median_concentration = median(result),
            sd_concentration = sd(result),
            IQR_concentration = IQR(result))
```

Figure 2 and the summary statistics show us large variations in the dangerous concentrations of bacteria in water sources in Austin. Mean concentrations of fecal streptococci are above the safe limit at 6072.42 colonies/100 mL with total coliform bacteria concentrations following close behind at 1299.784 colonies/100 mL. However, the standard deviation for each bacteria concentration is on the order of thousands and tens of thousands, implying that there are still many locations of dangerously high bacteria concentration.

Finally, we can look at the changing concentrations of bacteria over time in both surface and ground water sources.

```{r}
water_tidy |>
  filter(medium == 'Ground Water' | medium == 'Surface Water' & medium != 'Storm Water') |>
  ggplot() + #Make two plots for each water source of results as they change per year
  geom_point(aes(x = year, y = result, color = medium), show.legend = F) +
  facet_wrap(~medium) +
  labs(
    x = 'Year',
    y = 'Bacteria Concentration (colonies/100 mL)',
    title = 'Bacteria Concentration Since 1991 Across Water Sources',
    caption = 'Figure 3: Bacteria concentration since 1991 across water sources'
  ) +
  theme_bw()
  
water_tidy |> #Surface water averages
  filter(medium == 'Surface Water') |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(mean_concentration = mean(result))

water_tidy |> #Mean concentrations in colonies/100 mL, ground water averages
  filter(medium == 'Ground Water') |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(mean_concentration = mean(result))
```

Surface water concentrations are much more frequently reported than groundwater concentrations. Groundwater concentrations have stayed approximately the same since 1990. Surface water concentrations were extremely high in the 20th century (an average of 23713.57 colonies/100 mL in 1994) and have consistently improved in the 21st century (an average of 212.04 colonies/100 mL in 2010). However, there appears to be a slight uptick in concentration in recent years as shown by the right tail in Figure 3 of surface water concentrations.

## Time of Day Bacteria/Pathogen Samples Are Taken

In order to see what time of day bacteria samples are taken at, we must first look at the distribution of the time periods the data was acquired. We will find the number of samples collected per year to see this distribution.

```{r}
water_tidy |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = year), binwidth = 2, center = 1, fill = 'lightblue') +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1986, 2025, 3)) + #Show variations for every three years
  labs(
    x = 'Year',
    y = 'Frequency of Sample Collection',
    title = 'Distribution of Samples Collected over Time',
    caption = 'Figure 4: Distribution of samples collected over time'
  ) +
  theme_bw()

water_tidy |> #Count number of samples collected per year
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```

We see an approximately unimodal distribution where more samples were taken in the 90's and decreased in the 2000's. The most samples were taken in 2009 at 1857 samples. The least samples were taken in 1987 at 10 samples.

Next, we look at the distribution of samples taken per bacteria type. We can make a barplot for the distribution and compare across the bars.

```{r}
water_tidy |>
  group_by(parameter) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>
  ggplot() + #Bar plot showing number of samples that had a given bacteria concentration
  geom_bar(aes(x = count, y = parameter, fill = parameter), stat = 'identity', show.legend = F) +
  labs(
    x = 'Number of Samples',
    y = 'Type of Bacteria',
    title = 'Distribution of Bacteria Samples in Austin',
    caption = 'Figure 5: Distribution of bacteria samples in Austin, TX'
  ) +
  theme_bw()

water_tidy |>
  group_by(parameter) |> #count bacteria and percent in total
  summarize(count = n(),
            percent = 100*n()/nrow(water_tidy))
```

The bacteria that was found the most is E coli in 14852 samples while the least is enterococcus in only 167 samples. Next, we can find the hour at which the samples were taken for each type of bacteria.

```{r}
water_tidy |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(x = hour(date), fill = parameter), show.legend = F) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 2)) + # Change x axis to show more variation every 2 hours
  facet_wrap(~parameter) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = 'Hour Since Midnight',
    y = 'Number of Samples',
    title = 'Distribution of Samples per Day Across Bacteria Type',
    caption = 'Figure 6: Distribution of samples per day across bacteria type'
  )

water_tidy |> #Find number of samples taken per hour
  group_by(hour(date)) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```

For fecal streptococci, fecal coliform bacteria, and E coli, midnight is the most frequent time for sample collection (15988 samples). However, this is likely the default time entered for when the exact collection time is unknown. After the midnight peak, the next most frequent time is around 11 AM and noon (3165 samples).

## Bacteria/Pathogen Concentrations by Location

First, we will examine the distribution of bacteria/pathogen concentrations across Austin, Texas.

```{r}
# Exploring all bacteria/pathogen concentrations in relation to location of samples
water_tidy |>
  #Plot lat/long map
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = lon_dd_wgs84, y = lat_dd_wgs84)) +
  labs(
    x = 'Longitude (°)',
    y = 'Latitude (°)',
    title = 'Distribution of all Bacteria/Pathogen Concentrations across Austin',
    caption = 'Figure 7: Distribution of All Bacteria/Pathogen Concentrations across Austin'
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# Exploring all bacteria/pathogen concentrations in relation to location of samples by parameter
water_tidy |>
  # Filter out coordinates that are not in Austin
  filter(lon_dd_wgs84 != 0 | lat_dd_wgs84 != 0) |>
  #Plot lat/long map
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = lon_dd_wgs84, y = lat_dd_wgs84, color = parameter), show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = 'Longitude (°)',
    y = 'Latitude (°)',
    title = 'Distribution of Bacteria/Pathogen Concentrations across Austin by Parameter',
    caption = 'Figure 8: Distribution of Bacteria/Pathogen Concentrations across Austin by Parameter'
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter) +
  theme_bw()
```

From Figures 7 and 8, there are higher bacteria/pathogen concentrations in the central areas of Austin compared to the outer regions. This pattern suggests several potential factors. The central part of Austin contains a higher population density and increased human activity, which can contribute to the proliferation of bacteria and pathogens. Additionally, urban environments often have more sources of pollution and waste, which can create favorable conditions for microbial growth. The outer areas, being less densely populated and more suburban or rural, may have fewer such sources, leading to lower bacteria/pathogen concentrations.

## Safe Bacteria/Pathogen Concentrations Levels by Site Type

The US EPA sets specific recommendations for safe bacteria/pathogen concentrations in various water types to protect public health. These standards help ensure that water used for various purposes, from recreation to consumption, remains safe and free from harmful levels of pathogens. We will focus on three water types: recreational, treatment, and drinking.

Figure 9 is a distribution of bacteria/pathogen concentrations by site types in Austin, Texas.

```{r}
# Identifying the different site types
water_tidy |>
  group_by(site_type) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(y = site_type, fill = site_type), show.legend = F) +
  labs(
    x = 'Frequency of Site Type',
    y = 'Site Type',
    title = 'Distribution of Site Types',
    caption = 'Figure 9: Distribution of site types in Austin, TX'
  ) + 
  theme_bw()

water_tidy |>
  group_by(site_type) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```

### Recreational Water

For recreational water, we will look at site types lakes, springs, and streams because these waters are typically considered for recreational activities such as swimming, boating, and fishing. We will compare on E. coli and enterococcus concentrations with fecal coliform bacteria concentrations because the EPA emphasizes the former as better indicators.

```{r}
# Frequency of recreational water site types
water_tidy |>
  filter(site_type %in% c('Lake', 'Spring', 'Stream')) |>
  group_by(site_type) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```

The EPA's current standards in recreational water are a geometric mean of **no more than 126 colony-forming units (CFU) per 100 mL for E. coli** and a geometric mean of **no more than 35 CFU per 100 mL for enterococcus**. The EPA previously recommended a geometric mean of **no more than 200 CFU per 100 mL for fecal coliform bacteria**. In general, these thresholds are particularly significant for water used in activities where direct contact with skin is common. Maintaining below these amounts ensure that the water is safe for recreational use, reducing the risk of infections and other health issues associated with exposure to contaminated water.

Note: Colonies/per 100 mL is the same as CFU/100 mL.

Information on safe concentrations of E. coli and enterococcus in recreational water can be found here: <https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-10/documents/rec-factsheet-2012.pdf>. Information on safe concentrations of fecal coliform bacteria in recreational waters can be found here: <https://www.knowyourh2o.com/outdoor-4/fecal-coliform-bacteria-in-water>/

```{r}
# Comparing all three parameters in terms of safeness in recreational water
water_tidy |>
  filter(site_type %in% c('Lake', 'Spring', 'Stream')) |>
  filter(parameter %in% c("E COLI BACTERIA", "ENTEROCOCCUS", "FECAL COLIFORM BACTERIA")) |>
  mutate(safeness = case_when(
    parameter == "E COLI BACTERIA" & result <= 126 ~ T,
    parameter == "E COLI BACTERIA" & result > 126 ~ F,
    parameter == "ENTEROCOCCUS" & result <= 35 ~ T,
    parameter == "ENTEROCOCCUS" & result > 35 ~ F,
    parameter == "FECAL COLIFORM BACTERIA" & result <= 200 ~ T,
    parameter == "FECAL COLIFORM BACTERIA" & result > 200 ~ F)) |>
  ggplot() +
  #Plot lat/long map and color based on safety
  geom_point(aes(x = lon_dd_wgs84, y = lat_dd_wgs84, color = safeness)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "forestgreen")) +
  labs(
    x = 'Longitude (°)',
    y = 'Latitude (°)',
    title = 'Distribution Comparing Safeness Levels for Recreational Water',
    caption = 'Figure 10: Comparison of Safeness Levels for Recreational Water in Austin, TX'
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter) +
  theme_bw()

# Summary statistics
water_tidy |>
  filter(site_type %in% c('Lake', 'Spring', 'Stream')) |>
  filter(parameter %in% c("E COLI BACTERIA", "ENTEROCOCCUS", "FECAL COLIFORM BACTERIA")) |>
  mutate(safeness = case_when(
    parameter == "E COLI BACTERIA" & result <= 126 ~ T,
    parameter == "E COLI BACTERIA" & result > 126 ~ F,
    parameter == "ENTEROCOCCUS" & result <= 35 ~ T,
    parameter == "ENTEROCOCCUS" & result > 35 ~ F,
    parameter == "FECAL COLIFORM BACTERIA" & result <= 200 ~ T,
    parameter == "FECAL COLIFORM BACTERIA" & result > 200 ~ F)) |>
  group_by(parameter, safeness) |>
  summarize(count = n(), .groups = 'drop') |>
  group_by(parameter) |>
  mutate(parameter_count = sum(count),
         proportion = count/parameter_count)
```

For E. coli bacteria, 71.1% of the samples (9771 out of 13739) are considered safe for recreational use, and 28.9% of the samples (3968 out of 13739) are considered unsafe for recreational use. For enterococcus, only 5.3% of the samples (2 out of 38) are considered safe for recreational use, and 94.7% of the samples (36 out of 38) are considered unsafe for recreational use. For fecal coliform bacteria, 76.0% of the samples (10194 out of 13408) are considered safe for recreational use, and 24.0% of the samples (3214 out of 13408) are considered unsafe for recreational use. Therefore, the majority of samples for E. coli and fecal coliform bacteria are within safe levels for recreational water sites. However, a significant portion of enterococcus samples are above safe levels, indicating potential health risks for recreational activities in those waters.

### Domestic Water Supply

Domestic water supply refers to the provision of water for household uses such as drinking, cooking, cleaning, and bathing. This water typically comes from various sources, including wells, springs, lakes, and streams. Before it reaches homes, the water undergoes rigorous treatment processes to ensure it meets safety standards. These processes include filtration, sedimentation, and disinfection to remove contaminants and pathogens. Ensuring a reliable and safe domestic water supply is crucial for public health and well-being, as it prevents waterborne diseases and supports daily life activities. Proper management and treatment of water sources are essential to maintain the quality and availability of this vital resource.

For domestic water supply, we will look at site types lakes, springs, streams, drinking water tap, and wells. The EPA's current standard in domestic water supply is **fewer than 2000 colonies/100 mL**.

```{r}
# Frequency of domestic water supply site types
water_tidy |>
  filter(site_type %in% c('Lake', 'Spring', 'Stream', 'Well', 'Drinking Water Tap')) |>
  group_by(site_type) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```

Information on safe concentrations of fecal coliform bacteria in recreational waters can be found here: <https://www.knowyourh2o.com/outdoor-4/fecal-coliform-bacteria-in-water>/

```{r}
# Comparing all fecal coliform bacteria concentration levels for domestic water supply
water_tidy |>
  filter(site_type %in% c('Lake', 'Spring', 'Stream', 'Well')) |>
  filter(parameter == "FECAL COLIFORM BACTERIA") |>
  mutate(safeness = ifelse(result < 2000, T, F)) |>
  ggplot() +
  #Plot lat/long map and color based on safety
  geom_point(aes(x = lon_dd_wgs84, y = lat_dd_wgs84, color = safeness)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "forestgreen")) +
  labs(
    x = 'Longitude (°)',
    y = 'Latitude (°)',
    title = 'Distribution of Fecal Coliform Bacteria Safeness Levels in Domestic Water Supply',
    caption = 'Figure 11: Distribution of Fecal Coliform Bacteria Safeness Levels in Domestic Water Supply in Austin, TX'
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter) +
  theme_bw()

# Summary statistics
water_tidy |>
  filter(site_type %in% c('Lake', 'Spring', 'Stream', 'Well')) |>
  filter(parameter == "FECAL COLIFORM BACTERIA") |>
  mutate(safeness = ifelse(result < 2000, T, F)) |>
  group_by(site_type, safeness) |>
  summarize(count = n(), .groups = 'drop') |>
  group_by(site_type) |>
  mutate(site_type_count = sum(count),
         proportion = count/site_type_count)
```

For lakes, 95.4% of the samples (1092 out of 1145) are considered safe for domestic water supply, and 4.6% of the samples (53 out of 1145) are considered unsafe for domestic water supply. For springs, 99.9% of the samples (3469 out of 3472) are considered safe for domestic water supply, 0.1% of the samples (3 out of 3472) are considered unsafe for domestic water supply. For streams, 91.7% of the samples (8046 out of 8771) are considered safe for domestic water supply, 8.3% of the samples (725 out of 8771) are considered unsafe for domestic water supply. For wells, 98.0% of the samples (50 out of 51) are considered safe for domestic water supply, 2.0% of the samples (1 out of 51) are considered unsafe for domestic water supply. Therefore, the majority of samples from lakes, springs, streams, and wells are within safe levels for domestic water supply. This indicates that these sources are generally reliable for providing safe water for household use after appropriate treatment.

### Drinking Water

For drinking water, we will look at site types drinking water tap and well because these are typically considered direct sources of drinking water. The EPA's current standard in drinking water is the **absence of E. coli**.

Information on safe concentrations of E. coli bacteria in recreational waters can be found here: <https://www.knowyourh2o.com/outdoor-4/fecal-coliform-bacteria-in-water>/

```{r}
# Frequency of drinking water site types
water_tidy |>
  filter(parameter == 'E COLI BACTERIA') |>
  filter(site_type %in% c('Drinking Water Tap', 'Well')) |>
  group_by(site_type) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```

```{r}
# Comparing all E. coli concentration levels in drinking water
water_tidy |>
  filter(parameter == 'E COLI BACTERIA') |>
  filter(site_type %in% c('Drinking Water Tap', 'Well')) |>
  mutate(safeness = ifelse(result == 0, T, F)) |>
  ggplot() +
  #Plot lat/long map and color based on safety
  geom_point(aes(x = lon_dd_wgs84, y = lat_dd_wgs84, color = safeness)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "forestgreen")) +
  labs(
    x = 'Longitude (°)',
    y = 'Latitude (°)',
    title = 'Distribution of E. Coli Safeness Levels for Drinking Water ',
    caption = 'Figure 12: Distribution of E. Coli Safeness Levels for Drinking Water in Austin, TX'
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# Summary statistics
water_tidy |>
  filter(parameter == 'E COLI BACTERIA') |>
  filter(site_type %in% c('Drinking Water Tap', 'Well')) |>
  mutate(safeness = ifelse(result == 0, T, F)) |>
  group_by(site_type, safeness) |>
  summarize(count = n(), .groups = 'drop')
```

All drinking water sites have unsafe E. coli concentrations (greater than 0 CFU/100 mL or 0 MPN/100ML). Therefore, it would be hazardous to drink from these direct sources of water.

# Discussion

After conducting this analysis, we have a better picture of bacteria/pathogen concentrations in Austin. We can now see the changes across day and water source. To begin with, Figure 1 tells us that the majority of water sources are surface water sources (22531 sources). This tells us that our focus should be on testing surface water sources since they affect the most people. This is supported by Figure 3 where we see that almost all sampling has historically been done on surface water sources. However, Figures 3 and 4 also indicate that testing efforts have waned in the 21st century. While this is likely partly due to improved experimental analysis methods, it still represents a danger to the community since contamination could be missed with less testing.

To see the variations in a day, we can look to Figures 5 and 6. E coli bacteria are highly present in the samples, representing 14852 samples. Samples are most often taken in the late morning, between 11 AM and noon (ignoring the midnight category). The trend makes sense given that these times are during the workday and when most people are active. However, it is important to note that this is the warmest part of the day. Sampling methods will be affected by the temperature and properties of the water. Further research needs to be done on how this trend affects the measured bacteria concentration. The trends approximately agreed with expected findings of most frequent sampling happening during the day. We also did expect highest bacteria concentrations to appear in water sources closest to the outside environment. This was proven by the data and the dominance of surface water sources.

We can draw several important conclusions regarding the safeness levels of various water sources for both recreational and domestic use from Figures 10-12. For recreational water sites, the majority of samples for E. coli and fecal coliform bacteria are within safe levels, with 71.1% and 76.0% of samples respectively being safe. However, enterococcus contamination poses a significant risk, with only 5.3% of samples being safe. This highlights the need for improved water quality measures in recreational areas.

For domestic water supply, most sources such as lakes, springs, streams, and wells are generally safe, with high percentages of safe samples ranging from 91.7% to 99.9%. Nonetheless, occasional instances of unsafe samples from drinking water taps and wells underscore the importance of continuous monitoring and rigorous treatment processes to ensure the safety of domestic water supplies. Ensuring safe water for both recreational and domestic use is vital for preventing waterborne diseases and maintaining overall public health. Continuous efforts in monitoring, treatment, and management of water sources are essential to achieve this goal.

## Reflection

From the process, we have learned the importance of meticulous data analysis and the need for clear, concise communication. Interpreting data accurately is essential to draw meaningful conclusions and provide actionable insights. Moreover, this project underscored the significance of continuous monitoring and rigorous treatment processes to ensure water safety. It also highlighted the critical role of adhering to regulatory standards to protect public health.

Overall, this project has reinforced the value of detailed analysis, effective data interpretation, and the importance of maintaining high standards in water quality management.
